links.reason: Nothing at all is better than truthfulness, says one, yet the other ranks not killing first and puts not lying second.
links.quoteA: nothing at all is better than truthfulness
links.quoteB: Not killing stands alone as good. Next after it, not lying is good

links.reason: Where anger can take effect nothing is worse, says one, yet the other declares the carelessness of great delight worse than boundless rage.
links.quoteA: Where it can, nothing is worse
links.quoteB: Worse than boundless rage is the carelessness

links.reason: Someone who prizes anger will surely be ruined, yet the wise are shown burning within and watching for their time.
links.quoteA: Someone who prizes anger will be ruined
links.quoteB: They watch for the time and burn within

links.reason: Anger is wrong even when you cannot strike, yet the wise are praised for keeping theirs alive until they can.
links.quoteA: Anger is bad where it can’t take effect
links.quoteB: They watch for the time and burn within

links.reason: Those on the hill called virtue have an anger hard to withstand, yet renouncing anger is what makes you the equal of renouncers.
links.quoteA: The anger of those who stand on the hill called virtue is hard to withstand
links.quoteB: Those who renounce anger are the equals of renouncers

links.reason: Ruin from helping others is worth buying, even if you must sell up, yet helping without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth.
links.quoteA: that ruin is worth buying, even if you must sell up to do it
links.quoteB: Helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth

links.reason: Lavish your wealth and it is quickly gone for good, yet a benefactor's empty purse is called a passing drought, like a rain-cloud's.
links.quoteA: his substance will quickly come to nought
links.quoteB: only like the exhaustion of the rain-cloud

links.reason: Gifts must be kept in line with your means, yet old families are praised for going on giving after their means have shrunk.
links.quoteA: let thy gifts be commensurate therewith
links.quoteB: they give not up their liberality even when their means of munificence are diminished

links.reason: What fate makes yours won’t leave even if you throw it out, yet helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth.
links.quoteA: What is yours won’t leave, even if you throw it out
links.quoteB: Helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth

links.reason: Two flat reports on the same world: it doesn’t count a good person’s fall as ruin, and it scorns everyone who has nothing.
links.quoteA: The world does not count it ruin
links.quoteB: Everyone scorns those who have nothing

links.reason: Everyone scorns those who have nothing, yet the world is also said to count no lack as poverty except a lack of understanding.
links.quoteA: Everyone scorns those who have nothing
links.quoteB: The world does not count any other lack as poverty

links.reason: Those of an old family keep their good nature when their means shrink, yet poverty brings even them a weakness from which shameful words are born.
links.quoteA: those of an old family don’t part from their good nature
links.quoteB: Even in those of good family, poverty brings a weakness

links.reason: Uprightness and shame come by nature only to those of good family, yet birth is the same for all and only what they do sets them apart.
links.quoteA: Only in those born of a good family do uprightness and shame come together by nature
links.quoteB: Birth is the same for every living being

links.reason: Drive comes because fate is bringing wealth, or prosperity comes because someone’s drive never wavers: each makes the other’s effect its cause.
links.quoteA: The fate that brings you wealth also brings the drive to work
links.quoteB: Prosperity asks the way and goes by itself to someone whose drive never wavers

links.reason: The fate that takes wealth away brings laziness, yet making no effort is called your own disgrace, not fate’s.
links.quoteA: The fate that takes it away brings laziness
links.quoteB: The disgrace is to know what must be known and make no effort

links.reason: Compassion is the wealth above all wealth, and goods are found even among the low, yet compassion is said to thrive with wealth as its foster-mother.
links.quoteA: The wealth of compassion is the wealth among wealth
links.quoteB: thrives with the rich foster-mother called wealth

links.reason: The one who lives home life well is first among all who strive, yet those who renounce completely have arrived and all others are caught in a net.
links.quoteA: The one who lives home life as it should be lived is first among all who strive
links.quoteB: All others are deluded, and caught in a net

links.reason: Someone living home life rightly gains nothing from an outside path, yet you are also told to renounce while you can, for many things are yours then.
links.quoteA: what would you gain by going off on some outside path?
links.quoteB: renounce while you can

links.reason: Two accounts of what friendship is for: to reprove a friend who strays, or to be at ease and never resent his liberties.
links.quoteA: the restraining and reproving of oneself when one goeth astray
links.quoteB: To be free and easy with each other, that is the heart of true friendship

links.reason: For those who hold to friendship there is no leaving it once made, yet with those who spoil your work you are told to let it slowly slip away.
links.quoteA: once made there is no leaving it
links.quoteB: let the friendship slowly slip away

links.reason: A single evil word turns all your good bad, yet the noble may say things without goodness, so long as they say nothing useless.
links.quoteA: If a single evil word does its harm, the good you have done turns bad
links.quoteB: Let the noble say things without goodness if they will

links.reason: Hard words are allowed to the wise, yet the well-bred are said to be courteous even to enemies, since such words wound even in jest.
links.quoteA: speak even hard words
links.quoteB: never discourteous even to their foes

links.reason: Those who wrong you in their pride are to be conquered by your nobility, yet whoever fails to humble such pride will not last.
links.quoteA: Conquer by thy nobility
links.quoteB: those who humble not the pride of men who defy them

links.reason: Those who harm you are to be shamed with good and let go, yet those who despise you are to be kept laughing while the friendship dies within.
links.quoteA: do them such good that they are ashamed
links.quoteB: make them laugh, and within that friendship hold them so that it dies

links.reason: Think how you stand before the strong before you go against the weak, says one; the other tells you to seek enmity with the weak without holding back.
links.quoteA: When you go against those weaker than you, think of yourself before those stronger
links.quoteB: Without holding back, seek enmity with the weak

links.reason: When your adversary declines you may throw him down headlong, yet valour is said to take its edge from generosity to the fallen.
links.quoteA: thou mayest easily throw them down headlong
links.quoteB: chivalrous generosity to the fallen

links.reason: The weaker party is told to bend before its adversaries, and also that the day of decline is the day to hold fast to dignity.
links.quoteA: Bend down before thy adversaries
links.quoteB: in the day of thy decline hold fast to thy dignity

links.reason: The enmity of a man who does a task all wrong is worth paying for, yet the very next chapter says no one should want enmity, even in jest.
links.quoteA: Even if you must pay for it, be sure to get the enmity
links.quoteB: No one should want it, even in jest

links.reason: Don’t take another life even to save your own, yet a ruler who punishes the wicked with death is likened to someone pulling weeds from a green crop.
links.quoteA: don’t do what takes another sweet life
links.quoteB: A ruler who punishes the wicked with death is like someone pulling weeds from a green crop

links.reason: Doing wrong under a saintly garb is a fowler's trick, yet the prince's spies are told to go about disguised as ascetics and holy men.
links.quoteA: taketh cover under a saintly garb
links.quoteB: Spies and scouts shall disguise themselves as ascetics and holy men

links.reason: Saying you will think after you commit is a mistake, yet those who strive without delay for their family are promised success without planning.
links.quoteA: To say you will think after you have committed is a mistake
links.quoteB: success comes of itself, without planning

links.reason: A Councillor must always tell a thwarting prince what is right, yet whoever stands before the prince is told to say what pleases him.
links.quoteA: the duty of the Councillor is always to point to him what is just and proper
links.quoteB: Speak those things before the prince that are pleasant to him

links.reason: The wise won’t accept an unlearned man’s cleverness even when it is very good, yet understanding is seeing the reality in what you hear, from anyone.
links.quoteA: Even when an unlearned man’s cleverness is very good, the wise don’t accept it
links.quoteB: Whatever you hear, from whoever’s mouth, understanding is seeing the reality in it

links.reason: Desire as tall as a palmyra leaves no room for a millet seed of sulking, yet desire without sulks is like fruit too ripe or too green.
links.quoteA: you must not sulk even by a millet seed
links.quoteB: Without the deep sulk and the light one, desire is like a fruit too ripe and a fruit too green

links.reason: Remembering their days together is how she stays alive, yet keeping him in her heart, she says later, will only cost her more of her beauty.
links.quoteA: I live by remembering the days I was with him
links.quoteB: If we keep in our heart the one who left us and won’t come near, we will lose still more of our beauty

links.reason: When your means shrink you must stand tall, yet those raising a family are warned that thinking of their pride will ruin it.
links.quoteA: When your means shrink, stand tall
links.quoteB: Be idle and think of your pride, and it is ruined

links.reason: People can be red outside and black inside, yet the face, like crystal, is said to show what is strongest in the heart.
links.quoteA: red outside like the crab’s-eye seed, yet black inside
links.quoteB: the face shows what is strongest in the heart

links.reason: Men are to be judged by acts and not appearance, yet those who can judge intentions from looks are worth any price to a council.
links.quoteA: judge thou therefore men by their acts and not by their appearance
links.quoteB: judge a man’s intentions from his looks

links.reason: However much you study, the understanding you were born with wins out, yet understanding is also said to flow as far as you learn.
links.quoteA: the understanding you were born with still wins out
links.quoteB: People’s understanding flows as far as they learn

links.reason: Deeds don’t touch those devoted to the true praise of the Lord, yet your own deed is said never to go away, but to follow you and kill.
links.quoteA: do not touch those devoted to the true praise of the Lord
links.quoteB: The enemy that is your own deed never goes away

links.reason: Austerity is striven for because it brings what you want as you want it, yet craving can never be filled and is to be given up.
links.quoteA: what you want comes as you want it
links.quoteB: If you give up craving, whose nature is never to be filled

links.reason: Only those who do tapas serve their own good, and only those who till truly live: each couplet sets the other's man among the rest.
links.quoteA: It is the men that do tapas that look after their own interests
links.quoteB: They alone live who live by tilling the ground

links.reason: Many who didn’t know their strength broke halfway, yet you are told never to call a task too hard, because effort will give you greatness.
links.quoteA: set out on a surge of zeal and broke halfway
links.quoteB: Don’t lose heart and say “This is too hard.”

links.reason: Two exclusive claims meet here: only refuge at the Lord's feet crosses the ocean of births, and mercy is the only salvation.
links.quoteA: They alone cross the ocean of births and deaths
links.quoteB: Mercy is the only salvation

links.reason: Loss will always come, and only a heart that doesn’t lean sets the worthy apart, yet those who hold to compassion are said to have no misery.
links.quoteA: Loss and gain will always come
links.quoteB: Those who hold to compassion have no misery

links.reason: A rich man enjoys his wealth only as the Ordainer ordained, yet the man who does not enjoy his is called a disease on his fortune.
links.quoteA: cannot enjoy his riches except as the Ordainer hath ordained
links.quoteB: he is a disease unto a great fortune

links.reason: The poor may one day thrive, it is said, yet Destiny is also said to hold them to the miseries that are their portion.
links.quoteA: The poor in substance may one day thrive and prosper
links.quoteB: Destiny reserveth them for the miseries that are their portion

links.reason: Understanding is living as the world lives, yet those called the ocean of worth will not shift, even if the age itself does.
links.quoteA: However the world lives, understanding is living that way with the world
links.quoteB: Even if the age itself shifts, those called the ocean of worth will not shift

links.reason: Doubting someone you have come to trust brings endless suffering, yet a spy is there to watch everyone alike, even those who do your work and your kin.
links.quoteA: to doubt someone you have come to trust
links.quoteB: those who do your work, your own kin

links.reason: Enemies should be won over, faster even than friends are rewarded, or cut down young like thorn-trees before they can hurt you.
links.quoteA: Placate enemies
links.quoteB: Fell down thorn-trees while yet they are young

links.reason: A spear that missed an elephant beats an arrow that hit a hare, yet whoever won’t take the small prize of an easy fight will never win glory.
links.quoteA: Better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that hit a hare
links.quoteB: If you won’t take the small prize of fighting an unlearned man, glory will never come to you

links.reason: Puts a condition on the praise of learning as the great wealth that can’t be destroyed: without worship, it asks, what use is it?
links.quoteA: What use is learning to those who won’t worship
links.quoteB: Learning is the great wealth that can’t be destroyed

links.reason: Bearing with those who scorn you is called the highest thing, but holding back anger only counts where the anger could take effect.
links.quoteA: Whoever holds back anger where it can take effect truly holds it back
links.quoteB: the highest thing is to bear with those who scorn you

links.reason: A ruler’s honour must never slip from valour, but honour that has lost its nobility is itself counted among a ruler’s faults.
links.quoteA: honour that has lost its nobility
links.quoteB: an honour that never slips from valour

links.reason: Doing good however you can isn’t enough: even good can go wrong if it isn’t done knowing each person’s nature.
links.quoteA: Even doing good can go wrong, if you don’t do it knowing each person’s nature
links.quoteB: do righteous deeds everywhere they can be done

links.reason: Being without stain in your mind sounds like your own affair, but a pure mind is said to depend on pure company.
links.quoteA: A pure mind and pure deeds both depend on pure company
links.quoteB: To be without stain in your mind is all of righteousness

links.reason: Undercuts the four tests of a man: many who pass every test still change once they are actually doing the work.
links.quoteA: many people change with the nature of the work
links.quoteB: Test someone by these four, righteousness, wealth, pleasure and fear for their life, and then trust them

links.reason: Sets a limit on punishing the wicked like pulling weeds: a ruler must look into the wrong fairly and punish to fit it.
links.quoteA: looks into a wrong fairly and punishes to fit it
links.quoteB: A ruler who punishes the wicked with death

links.reason: Only kin are said to cherish old ties when you have lost everything, but an enemy within who is close by kinship brings harms that lead towards death.
links.quoteA: When an enemy within appears who is close by kinship, it brings many harms
links.quoteB: Only kin go on cherishing old ties even when you have lost everything

links.reason: Conditions the rule against opposing the strong: even the weak grow strong and win, if they know the place and guard themselves.
links.quoteA: Even the weak grow strong and win, if they know the place
links.quoteB: Keep from opposing the strong

links.reason: Softens the flat denial that the envious gain: a crooked heart does sometimes prosper, and that gives you something to think about.
links.quoteA: When a crooked heart prospers
links.quoteB: the envious have no gain

links.reason: Non-killing is called the greatest of virtues, yet here it is the saint's own virtue, with a different one set for the worthy man.
links.quoteA: The virtue of the saint is non-killing
links.quoteB: The greatest of virtues is non-killing

links.reason: Sulking may be the joy of desire, but it is like salt: drawing it out is a little too much.
links.quoteA: Drawing it out is like a little too much
links.quoteB: Sulking is the joy of desire

links.reason: Renown is made the point of appearing at all, but those who want glory with strength of character won’t do anything unworthy even for glory.
links.quoteA: won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory
links.quoteB: If you appear, appear with renown

links.reason: Courtesy of the tongue holds in both: no evil word even by a slip, no discourtesy even in enmity.
links.quoteA: can’t say evil things with their mouths, even by a slip
links.quoteB: stay courteous, even in enmity

links.reason: Both lift the shame from falling low on one condition: that you stay in the good, or have the strength called worth.
links.quoteA: does not count it ruin when someone who stays in the middle and in the good falls low
links.quoteB: Having nothing is no disgrace, if you have the strength called worth

links.reason: Both redefine poverty: to have plenty and turn a guest away is the real poverty, and the deepest kind.
links.quoteA: Poverty amid plenty is the folly of neglecting guests
links.quoteB: The deepest poverty is to turn a guest away

links.reason: The goad and the tortoise drawing in its limbs make one point: whoever masters the five senses lays up what is to come.
links.quoteA: guards the five senses with the goad called firmness
links.quoteB: draw in the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs

links.reason: Both single out speech as the thing above all to guard, because suffering, and even ruin, ride on its slips.
links.quoteA: Whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue
links.quoteB: guard carefully against any slip in your speech

links.reason: Both set sparing life above any gain: a thousand sacrifices are worth less than not killing, and gain that comes from killing is the lowest thing.
links.quoteA: Better than pouring offerings into a thousand sacrifices is not to take one creature’s life and eat it
links.quoteB: gain that comes from killing is the lowest thing

links.reason: Both call on the King of the Gods to prove the same thing: ascetic power can humble even Indra.
links.quoteA: The King of the Gods himself, Indra, is witness
links.quoteB: Even the king of the Gods will fail from his place

links.reason: He and she say the same thing of desire: it is a fire that burns when you move away, which no real fire can do.
links.quoteA: It burns when you move away and cools when you come near
links.quoteB: Can it burn when you leave it, as the sickness of desire does?

links.reason: The same moment told from each side: she barely moved from his embrace, he barely loosened it, and pallor came at once.
links.quoteA: I lay holding him and shifted a little
links.quoteB: When I loosened my arms in our embrace

links.reason: Desire outdoes liquor in the same way, heard first from him and then from her: liquor must be drunk, but desire delights at a glance.
links.quoteA: It can’t delight those who merely see, as desire does
links.quoteB: toddy can’t do this, but desire can

links.reason: Desire beats toddy in both for the same reason: merely thinking of it brings joy, and that is more than toddy can do.
links.quoteA: even thinking of it brings a great joy that doesn’t fade
links.quoteB: To be drunk at a thought

links.reason: Both are her own scolding of her heart: suffering over a man who has no love for you is foolish, as vain as filling in the sea.
links.quoteA: Fill in the sea instead
links.quoteB: He has no love for you, yet you go on suffering. That is foolishness, my heart

links.reason: Her heart is chided in both for the same disloyalty: it runs to the man who chose to leave and neglect her.
links.quoteA: you go after the one who left
links.quoteB: Even when you see he isn’t drawn to us, my heart, you go to him

links.reason: Both prefer modesty to jewels: it is the only true ornament of a man, and the ornament that makes trinkets needless on her.
links.quoteA: Modesty and a loving speech, these alone are the ornaments of man
links.quoteB: modesty as her especial ornaments

links.reason: Both make the friend who can rebuke you the one to seek, whether as protection from ruin or as a check when you stray.
links.quoteA: If you keep companions who will rebuke you
links.quoteB: Choose with care friends who, when you go wrong, can speak until you weep, rebuke you

links.reason: Wanting nothing is set above everything: a pride that breeds victory in one, a wealth with no equal here or there in the other.
links.quoteA: The pride of wanting nothing breeds victory
links.quoteB: There is no great wealth here to match wanting nothing

links.reason: Both give one rule for choosing what to do: turn down any undertaking that will not bring you real good.
links.quoteA: Don’t set your heart on deeds that bring no good
links.quoteB: keep away from work that doesn’t bring good along with fame

links.reason: Neither lets another's offence excuse your own: an insult gives no licence to slander, nor injustice to discourtesy.
links.quoteA: even though he hath insulted thee to thy very face
links.quoteB: even were it only against men who are unfriendly and unjust

links.reason: Both read a man's temper as the herald of his fate: a change in him shows which way Fortune is about to turn.
links.quoteA: when Fortune is about to smile on him
links.quoteB: When fortune is about to smile on a man

links.reason: Both warn off the same folly of taking on the mighty, which one simply forbids and the other calls beckoning to Death.
links.quoteA: Keep from opposing the strong
links.quoteB: For the powerless to harm the powerful is like beckoning Death with your hand

links.reason: Both measure love by a breath of air: the joy is an embrace that lets none through, and the pain is when one gets in.
links.quoteA: alloweth not even the air to come between
links.quoteB: a single breath of wind cut its way between us

links.reason: Even when the injury is deliberate and done in hate, both give the same answer: do not pay it back.
links.quoteA: Not harming in return, even when someone has harmed you in hatred
links.quoteB: it is best not to answer with harm out of strife

links.reason: Both go beyond not retaliating and ask for actual good to be done to the one who injured you.
links.quoteA: do them such good that they are ashamed
links.quoteB: What use is worth, if you don’t do kindness even to those who have done you harm?

links.reason: Nearly the same sentence twice: if you want to be free of ills, do no harm to others.
links.quoteA: If you don’t want painful things to strike you down, don’t do evil things to others
links.quoteB: Those who want to be free of pain cause none

links.reason: Both stay the hand by the same means: before you hurt another, remember how that hurt feels to you.
links.quoteA: think of yourself before those stronger
links.quoteB: What you know to be painful, you must not do to anyone else

links.reason: Both go past forgiving to forgetting: the best thing to do with an injury is to let it slip from memory.
links.quoteA: It is good to forget what is not good, that very day
links.quoteB: Forgetting it is better still

links.reason: Turn on your own faults the eye you keep for others’ and no harm can reach you, said first to everyone and later to the ruler.
links.quoteA: If you could see your own faults as you see strangers’ faults
links.quoteB: If a ruler removes his own faults first, and then looks at those of others

links.reason: Almost word for word: understanding is seeing the reality, in every thing and from every mouth.
links.quoteA: understanding is seeing the reality in it
links.quoteB: understanding is seeing the reality in it

links.reason: Both define the able mind by the same double skill: making yourself heard, and catching what others really mean.
links.quoteA: saying things so that they go home and are easy to grasp, and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say
links.quoteB: To speak so that others want to hear, and to take what is useful from what others say

links.reason: Learning that cannot be put across is called worthless in both: a flower with no scent, a scholar good for nothing.
links.quoteA: like flowers that bloom in clusters but have no scent
links.quoteB: of no use, however much they have learned

links.reason: Rule stays sound only if the ruler looks into it daily: do so every day, or watch the land go to ruin day by day.
links.quoteA: Let the ruler look into it every day
links.quoteB: When a ruler doesn’t look into things daily and do justice, his land goes to ruin day by day

links.reason: Giving trust or friendship without testing is the same mistake with a lasting price: suffering for those after you, or a sorrow that kills.
links.quoteA: Trust a stranger without testing them, and the suffering won’t end
links.quoteB: Someone who makes a friend without looking and looking again ends in a sorrow that kills him

links.reason: The person worth having is described in nearly the same words, well-born and dreading blame, first as one to trust and then as a friend.
links.quoteA: born of good family, free of faults, and has the shame that dreads a scar
links.quoteB: Someone well-born, who shrinks from blame upon himself

links.reason: Wealth won by stealing or deceit can’t hold, however it seems to grow: it perishes in one, and it is water in a pot of raw clay in the other.
links.quoteA: seems to grow, then perishes beyond all measure
links.quoteB: like pouring water into a pot of raw clay

links.reason: Gain made the wrong way is to be let go, however good it looks: give it up at once in one, let it roll away in the other.
links.quoteA: let go at once of gain that comes from leaving the middle
links.quoteB: don’t embrace it, let it roll away

links.reason: No necessity excuses a shameful act, not a hungry mother in one nor things you can’t do without in the other.
links.quoteA: Even if you see the mother who bore you go hungry, don’t do what the worthy condemn
links.quoteB: Even things you can’t do without, give them up if they would lower you

links.reason: Looks are no measure of a person, shown by the cruel arrow and the bent harp in one and by the axle pin of a great chariot in the other.
links.quoteA: Judge people the same way, by what they do
links.quoteB: Don’t scorn people for how they look

links.reason: A fort is only as good as those in it: there is no fort for those who are afraid, and none for those with no excellence in action.
links.quoteA: There is no fort for those who are afraid
links.quoteB: with those who have no excellence in action it is no fortress

links.reason: A high aim that fails beats a low one that succeeds: rising thoughts don’t truly fail, and a spear that missed an elephant outdoes an arrow in a hare.
links.quoteA: Even when it fails, it has the nature of not failing
links.quoteB: Better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that hit a hare

links.reason: Her answer to the village is the same in both: they say he has left her, but they cannot see where he is still with her.
links.quoteA: This town says he lives apart from me
links.quoteB: They say he left me in waking life

links.reason: What hurts her in both is not her own wasting but that people blame him for it.
links.quoteA: if people don’t spread it about that the one who won me is unkind
links.quoteB: I ache to hear him called cruel

links.reason: Both put real standing above outward rank: conduct makes a noble family in one, and sitting high makes no one high in the other.
links.quoteA: Good conduct is noble family
links.quoteB: Those who aren’t high aren’t high, even sitting high

links.reason: Both count winning over those not with you as sound policy, one urging haste and the other saying the world rests in such greatness.
links.quoteA: Be quicker to win over those not with you
links.quoteB: one whose nature is to make friends of enemies

links.reason: Both move the danger from the open enemy to the one who comes smiling as a friend.
links.quoteA: Fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within
links.quoteB: Fear the company of enemies who are like kin

links.reason: Both observe that a sound word fails if the speaker lacks standing, whether what he lacks is learning or money.
links.quoteA: even though it may be perfectly sensible
links.quoteB: will carry no weight even when they expound grand truths

links.reason: Both treat moving in step with the world as the test of understanding, which those who never learn it lack, however much else they learn.
links.quoteA: Those who don’t learn to move in step with the world
links.quoteB: understanding is living that way with the world

links.reason: Both show gain unhinging a small mind: the fool is a madman getting drunk, and distinction in the unworthy turns to nothing but excess.
links.quoteA: it is like a madman getting drunk
links.quoteB: when it falls to the unworthy, turns to nothing but excess

links.reason: Both say a man's own failing outdoes his enemies: envy ruins him where they spare him, and folly does what they could not.
links.quoteA: even if his enemies spare him, his own envy will work his ruin
links.quoteB: it is hard even for his enemies to cause him

links.reason: No prize justifies a stain on your name: not piled-up millions for those of good family, not the wide world for the best of people.
links.quoteA: Even for piled-up millions, those of good family won’t do anything that lowers them
links.quoteB: won’t want the wide world unless they have shame as their fence
